speaker_role: independent counselor / financial-aid consultant (Andy Lockwood, owner of a college planning business)
commercial_incentive: heavy: repeatedly promotes a free report and paid consultations at lockwoodcollegeprep.com
key_insights: Under the federal FAFSA formula, money held in a child's name (UTMA/UGMA custodial accounts) is assessed at up to 25% of the balance per year toward expected family contribution
Parent-owned assets, including 529 plans, are assessed at a much lower ~5.64% under the federal formula
Primary residence value, retirement accounts (401k/IRA/457), and the value of most small businesses for self-employed filers are FAFSA-exempt and should never be reported
Life insurance cash value and annuities are also FAFSA-exempt asset types
Many private colleges use their own institutional methodology and often treat 529 plans as a child's asset rather than a parent's, increasing their impact on aid eligibility at those specific schools
Presenter claims only about 19% of families actually hold a 529 plan despite its heavy marketing as a college savings vehicle
specific_numbers_or_facts: Custodial (UTMA/UGMA) accounts penalize aid eligibility up to 25% of the balance per year (presenter)
Parent-owned assets/529 plans penalize eligibility at 5.64% under the federal formula (presenter)
Presenter claims only 19% of families have a 529 account (source not given)
notable_or_distinctive: gives specific numeric FAFSA sheltering percentages (25% vs. 5.64%) rather than vague 'save in the right place' advice, and flags that many private colleges deliberately reclassify 529s as child assets
reliability_notes: presenter explicitly states he is not a financial advisor and gives only broad-strokes figures; video is essentially a lead-generation piece for paid consulting, and exact percentages/policies should be checked against current FAFSA/CSS Profile rules since these change over time
